edition: Issue 038: New Zealand votes, nobody wins, Parliament grows to fit everybody at 131 MPs, the All Blacks survive 40 scary minutes at Murrayfield, and Amazon CGI-snows Dunedin
tagline: Your 3-minute Sunday reset after the weirdest election night in MMP history: Labour won the most votes, National won the most seats, National's top ministers won the exit, and roughly 600,000 special votes will settle it by 27 November; the All Blacks spotted Scotland's hooker scoring a hat-trick and politely declined to be worried; and Amazon spent a fortune CGI-snowing Dunedin, where the true hero of the story is a five-minute walk.

stories.headline: Election night delivers what no poll predicted: a dead heat, a Parliament of 131, and National's senior MPs squeezed out by their own victory
stories.summary: With all places counted on election night, Labour won the party vote (29.4% to 29.2%) but National won more seats (42 to 36); the National-ACT-NZ First bloc sits on 67 seats in a record 131-MP Parliament, deputy Nicola Willis, Paul Goldsmith and Gerry Brownlee lost their list seats, Opportunity is in with 7 seats on 6.0%, and roughly 600,000 special votes will decide the government when official results land on 27 November.

body.text: The shortest possible reading of election night: New Zealand voted, and nobody won convincingly enough to stop arguing. With every polling place counted, Labour actually edged the party vote - 29.4 percent to National's 29.2 percent - but seats are what count under MMP, and there National came out ahead: 42 seats to Labour's 36. The preliminary tally hands the National-ACT-NZ First bloc 67 seats in a Parliament that has grown to 131 MPs - the largest in New Zealand history - courtesy of a double-barrelled overhang: National over-performed in the electorates, holding roughly 41 of the 44 seats it took in 2023, while Te Pāti Māori's five Māori seats arrived on a party vote of just 0.6 percent. Parliament's growth spasm brought a reshuffle of its own: with list seats squeezed by the overhang, deputy leader Nicola Willis, Paul Goldsmith and Gerry Brownlee are out, and Chris Bishop almost certainly too - a bloodbath the NZ Herald called 'incredibly challenging' - even as Christopher Luxon claimed 'a pathway to forming the next government'. Chris Hipkins told Labour's crowd: 'New Zealand has spoken... it may take us a little bit longer to figure out exactly what it is that you've said.' Winston Peters said: 'Don't get carried away.' Opportunity's Qiulae Wong - whose party reaches Parliament for the first time with seven seats on 6.0 percent - spent the campaign being told Luxon would not take her call; she may now be the only number he dials. Five electorates remain on a knife-edge, roughly 600,000 special votes are outstanding, and official results land on 27 November.

Consider this your briefing from the wing of the newsroom that reads polls for a living: electoral arithmetic can do almost anything, and overnight it chose to do everything at once. Labour won the most votes and finished second in seats. National finished first in seats while its most senior ministers were streamlined out of public life by their own party's victory - the overhang is what happens when a democracy's architecture keeps replying 'we'll build an extension', and it has now built Parliament bigger than a cruise ship with the same number of bathrooms. A party on 0.6 percent of the vote owns five seats and therefore roughly one whole coalition negotiation each. And the Kingmaker Who Was Ruled Out is now the country's most powerful inbox: until Saturday, 'Luxon will not take Wong's call' was a campaign position; today it's a coalition strategy. Last issue we had one sleep to wait. Now we have three weeks of insomnia, and every assumption written in the last three years gets re-plumbed like a bach over winter. 'The system has been gamed,' said Chlöe Swarbrick, correctly in the sense that everybody is now gaming it at once. The one poll we actually got right: the next Prime Minister is still a Chris. The good news is that whoever governs, the maths forces them to talk to people they spent a year not talking to - which is either democracy working, or revenge served by abacus. We'll know by Christmas. Popcorn is cheaper than a recount.

RNZ/Electoral Commission election-night results, 100% of places counted, preliminary (excludes special votes; published 8 Nov 2026): National 706,680 votes (29.2%, 42 seats), Labour 710,330 (29.4%, 36), Greens 321,902 (13.3%, 16), ACT 264,121 (10.9%, 13), NZ First 236,630 (9.8%, 12), Opportunity 144,298 (6.0%, 7), Te Pāti Māori 13,845 (0.6%, 5); 2,418,565 votes counted; provisional total 131 seats - the largest Parliament ever (previous record: 123 MPs in 2023, also from overhang). Bloc maths on those numbers: National+ACT+NZ First = 67 seats; Labour+Greens+Te Pāti Māori = 57; Opportunity (7) is the arithmetic key. RNZ analysis (Richard Shaw, The Conversation via RNZ, 8 Nov 2026) projects a Parliament of 129 or 130 MPs (the RNZ provisional tally sums to 131), puts the right bloc on a majority of about one or two seats, and lists three scenarios - a second-term coalition, a coalition requiring Opportunity's support, or a centre-left-plus-Opportunity arrangement - with special votes (nearly 600,000 at the last election, typically breaking left, this year including an unusually large overseas component) able to flip two or three seats. Official results due 27 November 2026; the next Parliament must sit by 14 January 2027 at the latest. Overhang (NZ Herald, 7 Nov): National's roughly six extra electorate seats and Te Pāti Māori's four extra combine for 11 seats beyond party-vote entitlement. Ministers out (RNZ/NZ Herald): deputy leader Nicola Willis, Paul Goldsmith, Gerry Brownlee; Chris Bishop 'in all probability'. Te Pāti Māori won 5 of 7 Māori electorates (Aperahama Edwards, Te Tai Tokerau; Oriini Kaipara, Tāmaki Makaurau; Hana-Rawhiti Maipi-Clarke, Hauraki-Waikato; Rawiri Waititi, Waiariki; Debbie Ngarewa-Packer, Te Tai Hauāuru). Quotes: Hipkins - 'New Zealand has spoken... it may take us a little bit longer to figure out exactly what it is that you've said' (RNZ); Luxon - 'a pathway to forming the next government' (NZ Herald); Peters - 'Don't get carried away' (NZ Herald); Swarbrick - the overhang push and enrolment-law changes show 'the system has been gamed' (NZ Herald). Knife-edge electorates: Stuff (8 Nov) counts five still uncalled, including Hamilton East (National's Ryan Hamilton +456 over Labour's Georgie Dansey); NZ Herald calls Mt Roskill too close to call. Luxon said during the campaign he would not answer a call from Opportunity leader Qiulae Wong (RNZ/The Conversation).

stories.headline: All Blacks 43, Scotland 21: the 121-year streak survives a Scottish hooker's hat-trick and 40 minutes of genuine alarm at Murrayfield
stories.summary: The All Blacks beat Scotland 43-21 at Murrayfield to stay unbeaten (4-0) in the Nations Championship, scoring seven tries - including a Beauden Barrett brace, his 49th and 50th in tests - after trailing 24-21 at halftime; Scotland's Ewan Ashman scored a hat-trick, the first non-Australian or South African to do so against New Zealand, before a 19-0 second half ended the fun.

body.text: The All Blacks' week in Edinburgh started badly, got worse, and spent 40 minutes trying to stay that way before normal service resumed with the scoreboard's permission. New Zealand beat Scotland 43-21 at Murrayfield on Sunday (NZT) - a seven-try bonus-point win that keeps Dave Rennie's side unbeaten at 4-0 in the Nations Championship, level on competition points with South Africa, who had earlier put 66 points on Italy in Rome. For a half, the 121-year record looked genuinely mortal. The All Blacks turned at halftime only 24-21 up after two All Blacks sin-bins and an outright coup: Scottish hooker Ewan Ashman scored three tries, the first player outside Australia and South Africa to bag a hat-trick against New Zealand. Scotland, in their 34th attempt at a first-ever win, had every excuse to believe. Then came the second half: 19 unanswered points, Beauden Barrett's second try his 50th in test rugby, and wing Josh Moorby and replacement hooker Asafo Aumua adding gloss off an attacking lineout. Wallace Sititi, Ethan de Groot and Codie Taylor supplied the first-half tries. The win is not entirely clean: Will Jordan departed with what looked like a recurrence of a hamstring issue, and Jordie Barrett took a nasty head-to-shoulder hit.

Scotland, on behalf of a country that had already spent its entire weekend nail-biting budget on an election: thank you for the most stressful 40 minutes of the year. A hat-trick against the All Blacks from a hooker is the rugby equivalent of the person in front of you at the supermarket checkout suddenly hoisting the whole deli counter on his own - Ewan Ashman did everything short of erecting a small cairn on the try line, and it still wasn't enough, because the All Blacks spent halftime calmly agreeing to be the All Blacks again, and the second half went 19-0. Beauden Barrett scored his 50th test try with the same expression a man wears when the coffee he ordered eight minutes ago finally arrives: inevitable, mildly satisfying, superbly timed. There was one scrum in the entire first half - a world record for a code with an entire discipline named after it, and we'd like to file a complaint on behalf of every front-rower who turned up for a bake and got a walk. The All Blacks stay level with the Boks on points, though South Africa's 66-7 demolition of Italy lurks in the differential column like that friend who calculates who owes whom at brunch to the cent. Scotland: 34 attempts, 121 years, zero wins - the longest unrequited crush in sport, and we'll be sorry when it finally happens, because some streaks you only appreciate the week before they end.

RNZ (Patrick McKendry, 8 Nov 2026, 'New Zealand outclass Scotland to maintain unbeaten record'): All Blacks 43 (tries: Beauden Barrett 2 - his 49th and 50th test tries - Wallace Sititi, Ethan de Groot, Codie Taylor, Josh Moorby, Asafo Aumua; Damian McKenzie 4 conversions), Scotland 21 (Ewan Ashman 3 tries; Finn Russell 3 conversions). Halftime 24-21; Scotland scoreless in the second half, which finished 19-0 per The Post. Sin-bins: Peter Lakai (NZ, 24 min), Wallace Sititi (NZ, 33 min), Scotland captain Sione Tuipulotu (51 min). Only one scrum in the first half (RNZ). Streak: Scotland have never beaten New Zealand in 34 tests over 121 years (RNZ/NZ Herald); Ashman's hat-trick is the first by a non-Australian or South African against the All Blacks (NZ Herald). Nations Championship: New Zealand 4-0 and level on competition points with South Africa (66-7 winners over Italy in Rome), who lead on points differential (RNZ/The Post). Injuries: Will Jordan departed with what appeared to be a recurrence of his hamstring issue; Jordie Barrett left after a head-to-shoulder collision (NZ Herald). Match played Sunday 8 November NZT at Murrayfield; Dave Rennie in his first season as All Blacks head coach (RNZ).

stories.headline: Amazon's big-budget Christmas miracle is set in Dunedin, where the most heroic journey is a five-minute walk and the penguins are AI
stories.summary: Amazon released its big-budget Christmas campaign, filmed in Dunedin, on Friday: CGI snow falls on the southern city, a heritage bus plays the Beatles, AI penguins sit at Aramoana, Port Chalmers's port is digitally erased, and the heroine takes a boat across what Stuff's fact-check confirms is a five-minute walk - all before 'Mom' (US spelling) opens the door on Stafford Street.

body.text: Amazon has released its big-budget Christmas campaign, and Dunedin is once again standing in for every winter anywhere in the world. The ad, out Friday, follows a young woman whose flight is cancelled by copious and extremely digital snow falling on the southern city; from there she donates her family's presents to a succession of wonderfully helpful strangers across Otago's most photogenic corners. Stuff's Hamish McNeilly fact-checked the film the way only a local could. The heroine waits for a bus at an off-ramp on the wrong side of the road, wearing a red beanie given to her by an airport worker - which raises what McNeilly calls the obvious question: 'You're in Dunedin now, where is your own bloody beanie and puffer jacket?!' She boards a heritage Dunedin bus to the Beatles' Golden Slumbers ('Once there was a way to get back home'), gifts her dad's woollen socks to a couple whose own socks have holes in them after riding a boat across 'large swells' from Careys Bay to Port Chalmers - a five-minute walk, and, per McNeilly, 'you just wasted your dad's present on nothing and were taken for a literal ride by some locals'. She then takes the 'world's smallest taxi' with the 'world's largest taxi driver' on a roughly 30-kilometre trip to Otago Peninsula that ends back in the city, before finally delivering the one present that survives - addressed to 'Mom', American spelling - to a house on Stafford Street. Keyhole Rock at Aramoana features with companion penguins that are, McNeilly ascertains, AI. It is, he concludes, clearly 'big budget' - 'but what a journey'.

It's the most wonderful time of the year for a megacorporation to spend enormous money on weather that does not occur: Amazon has solved snowfall in the one place on Earth where the locals have spent a century explaining that the frost is beautiful, genuine, and free. The film is a joy in the sense that the entire civic infrastructure of a small southern city has been converted into geo-tagged Narnia: the penguins are AI, the working port has been photoshopped into the sea, and the world's smallest taxi runs a metered odyssey that ends exactly where it started - which we're fairly confident is also the plot of the Prime video terms and conditions you accepted in 2019. But the true hero is the five-minute walk: Careys Bay to Port Chalmers is a genuinely lovely stroll, and the film renders it as an Atlantic crossing, which says everything about how film budgets say goodbye to geography. And let us raise a beanie to the heroine herself: no personal puffer jacket, standing on the wrong side of the road in an off-ramp blizzard, carrying gifts chosen by someone with strong opinions about her in-laws. The perils of the family Christmas are indeed universal, and Amazon has spent a fortune to remind us all that the hardest part of the season is getting home with your own socks still intact. Joy delivered - take the walk sometime, Dunedin's is nicer than the CGI.

Stuff (Hamish McNeilly, 6 Nov 2026, 'Snow place like home: Fact checking the big budget Amazon Xmas commercial filmed in ye olde Dunedin'): Amazon released its Christmas campaign, filmed in Dunedin, on Friday 6 November 2026. Elements verified in the piece: the flight-cancelling snow is CGI-generated; the heroine receives a red beanie from an airport worker and waits at an off-ramp on the wrong side of the road; she boards an old heritage Dunedin bus with 'Golden Slumbers' by The Beatles playing; locations include Aramoana's Keyhole Rock (also known as Bear Rock) with penguins the article describes as AI-generated, Careys Bay, and Port Chalmers - whose working port is digitally erased in the film and which McNeilly clocks as about a five-minute walk from Careys Bay; a taxi described as 'the world's smallest taxi' carries her to Otago Peninsula (passing Pineapple Rock, roughly a 30km journey) and returns her to the city; the film ends at a house on Stafford Street, Dunedin, where 'Mom' (US spelling) opens the door, with the on-screen caption 'Joy delivered'. Stuff does not publish a budget figure - 'big-budget' is Stuff's description. Related precedent: Stuff previously reported ('The Deep South doubles as "The North" for UK Xmas commercial') that Dunedin had doubled as a winter stand-in for a UK Christmas TV commercial.

affiliate_cta.headline: The country is in a three-week waiting room - if you are about to spend while we all wait, here is the calm look-around.
affiliate_cta.body: Today's theme is waiting: a country waiting for special votes and a government by 27 November, rugby fans waiting a week to find out whether two Barretts are okay, and Dunedin waiting for snow that only ever arrives by pixels. If any of that has you about to commit to a purchase - a new sofa for coalition-watching, a puffer jacket, a plane ticket to anywhere with real weather - take a calm look around before you sign. No pitch, no pressure, just the specs.

rnz.co.nz / The Conversation (Richard Shaw, 'A knife-edge result, 3 possible outcomes', 8 Nov 2026): right bloc 67 vs left 56 in his count; parliament '129 or 130'; right bloc majority c.1-2 seats; three scenarios; specials ~600k at last election, typically break left; Luxon ruled out taking Wong's call; parliament must sit by 14 Jan 2027.

nzherald.co.nz (7 Nov 2026, 'Election 2026 live updates: Overhang and Opportunity in boxseat as results deadlocked' + topic page): Luxon 'pathway to forming the next government'; Willis, Goldsmith, Brownlee out, Bishop 'in all probability'; ministers' losses 'incredibly challenging'; overhang ~11 seats combined (National ~6, TPM ~4); Swarbrick 'the system has been gamed'; TPM won 5 of 7 Maori electorates; ACT 10.9%/13 seats - 'third record result in a row'.

stuff.co.nz (8 Nov 2026, 'Five electorates still on a knife-edge after election night'): Hamilton East - National's Ryan Hamilton leads Labour's Georgie Dansey by 456; five electorates uncalled. Also 'Utterly bizarre election leaves no winner. Here's what could happen next'.

rnz.co.nz (Patrick McKendry, 8 Nov 2026, 'New Zealand outclass Scotland to maintain unbeaten record'): All Blacks 43-21 Scotland at Murrayfield, HT 24-21, Scotland scoreless in 2nd half; 7 NZ tries incl. Barrett brace (49th/50th); Ashman hat-trick; sin-bins Lakai/Sititi/Tuipulotu; one scrum in first half; 4-0 Nations Championship, level with SA (66-7 v Italy), Boks ahead on differential; 'most difficult week in Edinburgh'.

nzherald.co.nz (7-8 Nov 2026, 'The All Blacks beat Scotland 43-21 at Murrayfield'): 34th test, 121-year unbeaten record vs Scotland; Ashman first non-Aus/SA hat-trick against NZ; Will Jordan hamstring recurrence concern; Jordie Barrett head-to-shoulder collision.

stuff.co.nz (Hamish McNeilly, 6 Nov 2026, 'Snow place like home: Fact checking the big budget Amazon Xmas commercial filmed in ye olde Dunedin'): Amazon Christmas campaign filmed in Dunedin, released Fri 6 Nov; CGI snow, wrong-side-of-road bus stop, Beatles 'Golden Slumbers', Careys Bay-Port Chalmers five-minute walk rendered as a sea voyage, world's smallest taxi to Otago Peninsula, AI penguins at Aramoana, erased Port Chalmers port, 'Mom' on Stafford St; 'Joy delivered'. Stuff also previously covered Dunedin doubling as 'The North' for a UK Christmas commercial.
